🗣️ the client's own words

items.prompt: Why does "cut double-booking incidents from 4 a quarter to 0" persuade more than "significantly reduced errors"?
choices: It's specific and checkable, where the vague version could describe almost any outcome
It uses more technical vocabulary, which makes it sound more credible to a reader skimming for expertise
It's a shorter sentence, and shorter claims tend to read as more confident than longer, hedged ones
It mentions a dollar figure, and the vague one doesn't, even though neither actually names a real client
items.explanation: The specific number is a concrete, falsifiable fact; the vague phrase could describe almost any result, including a disappointing one, so a skeptical reader has no way to tell the difference and discounts it by default.
items.reference:
💬 vague: "significantly reduced errors"
🔢 specific: "4 incidents a quarter to 0"

Why: A vague claim is unfalsifiable, so skeptical readers discount it by default; a specific, checkable number is much harder to wave away.

items.explanation: Because the claim can't be checked, a prospect has no way to distinguish it from ordinary marketing language, so their default is to give it the same weight as any other unverified promotional claim.
items.reference:

🔢 specific: "4 incidents a quarter to 0"

Why: A vague claim is unfalsifiable, so skeptical readers discount it by default; a specific, checkable number is much harder to wave away.

Anonymous claims are always shorter, so readers spend less time evaluating whether the detail actually holds up

items.explanation: A named, specific detail reads as something that actually happened, because it's the kind of thing a person could verify — an anonymous, generic version gives the reader nothing to check against.

🔢 specific: "4 incidents a quarter to 0"

Why: Persuasion doesn't require a public logo — it requires a real person a prospect can talk to. The referral loop survives on private introductions alone.

items.prompt: According to L3's extension, does persuasion actually require a public, named case study?
choices: No — it requires a real person a prospect can talk to, which a private reference call can still provide
Yes — an anonymous case study is never persuasive under any circumstances, regardless of how it's structured
Yes, but only if the client's company is well-known enough that the anonymity doesn't actually hide much
No, because numbers alone are always sufficient with no client involvement needed at any point in the process
items.explanation: The persuasive power comes from a real, specific person a prospect can verify and talk to — a public logo is one way to signal that, but a private reference call built on the same real numbers and quote works just as well.

items.prompt: If Fairmont's real result had been a 50% reduction in incidents rather than 100%, what does L3 say the case study should do?
choices: State the real number plainly and explain the gap honestly, rather than inflating the figure to look more dramatic
Round the number up to make it sound closer to a full elimination, since readers respond better to bigger claims
Skip publishing a case study entirely, since the result isn't dramatic enough to be worth the effort of writing one
Combine it with a different client's stronger result to make one impressive case study out of the two separately
items.explanation: An honest, modest number a prospect can verify is more persuasive over time than an inflated one that doesn't hold up — the same lesson value-based-selling draws from a vendor whose exaggerated promise cost more in trust than a smaller honest number would have.
items.reference:
📊 honest 50% reduction stated plainly, with the gap explained
🚫 vs. an inflated number that doesn't hold up under a prospect's questions

Why: A modest, verifiable number beats an inflated one — the trust lost when a promise doesn't hold up costs more than a smaller honest number ever would.

items.prompt: In the modest-result extension, how does L3 say the referral ask itself should change if the result is solid but not dramatic?
choices: Narrow it to prospects whose situation most closely matches the part of the result that's actually strong
Stop asking for referrals altogether until a more dramatic result is achieved somewhere else in the account
Broaden it to as many contacts as possible to compensate for the weaker number with sheer volume of asks
Ask the client to inflate the number when describing it to their contacts, to make the story land harder
items.explanation: Rather than broadcasting a modest result broadly, aiming the ask at the prospects whose situation most closely matches the strong part of what actually happened keeps the pitch honest and still persuasive.

items.prompt: Why does L3 compare the modest-result scenario to the inflated $92,000-promised, $30,000-delivered example from value-based-selling?
choices: Both illustrate that an exaggerated claim costs more in lost trust than a smaller, honest number would have cost in a first impression
Both examples involve the exact same client and deal, just described from two different angles in the write-up
Both show that dramatic numbers should always be used whenever possible, since bigger claims persuade more readers
Both are examples of a case study that should never be published at all, since neither result was dramatic enough
items.explanation: The parallel makes the same point in a different context: a claim that later needs walking back damages credibility more than a modest, accurate claim that holds up — which is exactly the trade-off facing a case study describing a real but unspectacular result.
